items.title: WHEN WORKERS AGREE WITH EVERYTHING: ACQUIESCENCE, WORDING EFFECTS AND THE MEASUREMENT OF GIG WORKER WELLBEING
items.abstract: Interviewer-administered surveys are the dominant method for studying the working lives of low-income and informal workers in the Global South, but the response styles they elicit have received scant attention. This study investigates acquiescence—the tendency to agree with statements irrespective of content—and wording effects in a survey of 887 delivery and ride-hailing workers in Mumbai, India. Negatively worded wellbeing items did not function as reversed wellbeing indicators, but loaded as a different work strain factor. A random intercept factor accounting for acquiescence explained about 16% of the variance in each item. Acquiescence, without correction, masked substantively important relationships: job demands were unrelated to wellbeing (r = −.04), whereas the expected strong negative relationship was observed after correction (r = −.54), similarly for income instability, platform dependency and job resources. The effect was replicated in an independent half of the sample that was not used to develop the measurement model and was, if anything, stronger (from −.08 to −.70). The scales showed full scalar invariance across quick commerce and food delivery workers. Because acquiescence inflates negatively and positively worded statements, it cancels out inverse relationships, and does not simply inflate positive relationships. Therefore, uncorrected survey research on low-income workers is subject to reporting null findings where real relationships exist . We provide practical advice on how to design, carry out and analyse such surveys.

items.title: Zero or Hero? Exploring the Use of AI Tools for Thematic Analysis in Science Communication Evaluation
items.abstract: Practitioners in informal science learning institutions are often expected to analyse evaluation data with limited time and expertise, and some are turning to artificial intelligence (AI) tools for support. To examine what these tools can realistically offer, we used interview data from an outreach event. We compared single-prompt thematic analyses produced by five AI tools with each other and with an iterative practitioner–AI analysis. We also explored how qualitative researchers judged the feasibility, trustworthiness and practical value of AI support. The AI tools consistently identified core patterns, but their outputs were largely descriptive, varied across trials and included hallucinated quotes. We recommend a hybrid approach in which AI assists with organising data while researchers retain responsibility for interpretation.

items.title: "It Feels Weird to Just Rely on AI": How Experienced Healthcare Professionals Work With Decision Support Systems in Clinical Practice
items.abstract: Decision support systems (DSS) assist with clinical decision-making. Little is known, however, about the decision-making process with DSS in clinical practice and the extent to which clinicians consider or rely on the predictions. Studies on human-AI decision-making usually focus on laypeople, simplified decision tasks, or one-shot interactions with prototypes that are not integrated into existing workflows. To gain insights from real-world practice, we conducted an online survey (n=12) and semi-structured interviews (n=10) with clinicians from two different medical cohorts each working with a DSS. Findings show, amongst other things, that the interaction with DSS changes as experience increases, the predictions become more important in complex cases, that decisions are discussed with colleagues, and that workflow integration affects decision-making. Our findings on human, technical, contextual, and organisational factors contribute to a socio-technical perspective on DSS reliance behaviour. We conclude by discussing the implications of our findings for the design of DSS.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

items.title: (How) Do Machines Make Sense? Respecifying Meaning in LLM-based Conversational AI
items.abstract: In this paper I revisit the question of whether machines "make sense" by respecifying meaning through an ethnomethodological perspective. Rather than treating meaning as a cognitive state or semantic property, ethnomethodology conceptualizes it as an emergent accomplishment of social interaction. Drawing on this approach, the paper argues that large language model (LLM)–based conversational AI should be evaluated not in terms of whether it “truly” understands or produces “genuinely” meaningful utterances, but in terms of how it participates in producing, maintaining, and repairing interactional order. While machines still struggle with tasks such as common sense reasoning or grasping irony and humor, they excel at one thing: maintaining the flow of conversation even at the cost of "bullshitting". In this paper, I argue that this emergent behavior, often dismissed as a failure, should instead be understood as a distinctive mode of engagement that signals contemporary artificial agents’ capacity to participate in meaning-making. A “mechnomethodology” shifts attention from how humans make sense of AI to how artificial agents make sense of, to, and with humans and other machines, thereby encouraging empirical investigation of machines’ meaning-making rather than metaphysical speculation about internal cognition or the status of their utterances.

items.title: A Conceptual Design Framework for Integrating Smart PPE Monitoring with Proposed Predictive Analytics in Smart Manufacturing Safety Management
items.abstract: Manufacturing safety is being digitalized through wearable sensors, connected-worker platforms, and artificial intelligence (AI), but the evidence does not yet justify treating a conceptual architecture as a validated predictive safety system.This study therefore proposes a conceptual design framework for integrating smart personal protective equipment (PPE) monitoring with future predictive analytics in smart manufacturing.We conducted a structured integrative synthesis of peerreviewed literature published from 2018 through September 2026 in Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and ScienceDirect, supplemented by targeted searches of occupational safety agencies, standards bodies, and primary manufacturer documentation.Search concepts combined smart PPE or workplace wearables with occupational safety, manufacturing, ergonomics, human-robot collaboration, IoT, anomaly detection, and machine learning.Sources were assembled by theoretical sampling from anchor reviews and their citation networks, and selection stopped at conceptual saturation of the framework's design space rather than at exhaustive coverage of the field.We coded eligible sources by industrial sector, hazard, sensing modality, connectivity, analytical method, validation maturity, and governance coverage against a published codebook.We organized recurrent capture-transmit-analyzeact functions into four technical layers.We linked them to a cross-cutting governance and assurance plane covering accountability, worker participation, purpose limitation, data access and retention, human decision authority, and algorithmic oversight.The resulting conceptual outputs distinguish calibrated rule-based alerts, statistical anomaly detection, supervised hazard classification, and prognostic modeling; specify candidate inputs, ground-truth labels, and validation metrics; and define controls for sensor drift, missing data, latency, false alarms, model drift, uncertainty, and alert fatigue.Numeric operational thresholds are intentionally excluded because no sensor system, dataset, simulation, or field trial was used.The contribution is therefore a traceable design framework and staged research agenda, not evidence of predictive performance or safety improvement.Future work must calibrate sensors, prospectively validate models across worker subgroups, evaluate human factors and privacy, and demonstrate that the system remains advisory relative to independently engineered safety controls.

items.title: A Cross-National Comparison of Physical Fitness, Physical Activity, and Motivational Climate Among Adolescent Girls in Iran and Hungary
items.abstract: This study compared physical fitness, physical activity, and motivational climate among adolescent girls in Iran and Hungary within the frameworks of self-determination theory and achievement goal theory. A cross-sectional study was performed among 539 girl students aged 13–15 years (mean age = 13.93; SD = 0.82 years). Data were analysed using factorial ANOVA, independent t-tests, confirmatory factor analysis, and structural equation modelling. Hungarian students demonstrated higher performance in most physical fitness tests and had higher body mass index values (p = 0.002). Physical activity levels differed only at age 14 (p = 0.019, r = −0.18), with no significant differences at other ages. Iranian students reported higher perceptions of motivational climate dimensions. The measurement model showed good fit (χ2(143) = 1.81; CFI = 0.99; TLI = 0.99; SRMR = 0.03; RMSEA = 0.039), and structural equation modelling indicated that only task-involving climate was positively associated with physical activity (β = 0.325, p = 0.003), while other motivational dimensions were not significant. The findings demonstrated that although physical fitness and motivational climate dimensions differed across both countries, physical activity levels remained relatively similar among groups. This implies that intrinsic motivational climate may be related to physical activity participation. However, differences in physical activity levels in each country could be attributed to other variables such as education, culture, socioeconomic status, environment, among others. Task-involving climate emerged as the only dimension of motivational climate associated significantly with physical activity, suggesting a potential association between task-involving climate and active lifestyles among adolescent girls.

items.title: A METHODOLOGY FOR IMPROVING TEACHING EFFECTIVENESS THROUGH ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE-INTEGRATED DIGITAL LEARNING PLATFORMS
items.abstract: This article examines the pedagogical and methodological aspects of improving teaching effectiveness through digital learning platforms integrated with artificial intelligence (AI). It analyzes the didactic potential of AI technologies in digital learning environments, the organization of learning processes adapted to students’ individual needs, the development of independent learning activities, and mechanisms for assessing knowledge and learning outcomes. The article also explores the application of AI tools in adaptive, blended, distance, synchronous, and asynchronous learning. A methodological approach aimed at improving teaching effectiveness through the integration of AI into digital learning platforms is proposed. The main components of this approach, criteria for assessing effectiveness, existing challenges, and possible solutions are discussed. The proposed methodology emphasizes the integration of digital platforms, AI tools, pedagogical strategies, and assessment mechanisms within a unified educational framework.

items.title: A Multi-Method Adaptive Ergonomic Framework for Mitigating MSDs among Pre-Elderly Workers in MSMEs
items.abstract: Purpose: This study aims to develop and evaluate an adaptive ergonomic framework for reducing Musculoskeletal Disorder (MSD) risks among pre-elderly workers in Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs). Methodology: This study adopted a sequential quantitative design consisting of two consecutive phases. The first phase involved a cross-sectional ergonomic assessment of 50 pre-elderly MSMEs workers using the Nordic Body Map (NBM), Rapid Entire Body Assessment (REBA), Rapid Upper Limb Assessment (RULA), and Quick Exposure Checklist (QEC). Based on the integrated assessment results, an adaptive ergonomic framework incorporating administrative controls, engineering controls, ergonomic personal protective equipment (PPE), and anthropometry-based workstation redesign was developed. The second phase evaluated the framework through a 14-day before–after intervention study in five selected MSMEs. Results: Most workers were exposed to moderate-to-very high ergonomic risks, with musculoskeletal complaints predominantly affecting the lower back, back, wrists, neck, and lower extremities. Following implementation, QEC exposure scores decreased across the five MSMEs from 68.7–84.5% before intervention to 46.3–63.2% after intervention, accompanied by reductions in REBA/RULA risk classifications and lower NBM complaint levels. Conclusion: The proposed framework effectively reduced ergonomic risks and musculoskeletal complaints among pre-elderly MSMEs workers through practical and low-cost interventions. Originality: This study contributes a comprehensive and context-specific adaptive ergonomic framework that integrates risk assessment, workstation redesign, administrative controls, and ergonomic PPE recommendations tailored to the characteristics of pre-elderly workers in resource-constrained MSMEs.

items.title: A Qualitative Study on a Hybrid Human–AI Model in the Workplace Based on Socio-Technical Systems Theory
items.abstract: The aim of this study is to examine individuals’ views and expectations regarding the hybrid human–artificial intelligence relationship that could be established in the workplace within the Turkish context. The study was conducted using a qualitative research design. A semi-structured questionnaire was used. Data were analysed using the Straussian grounded theory approach through open, axial and selective coding. A total of 92 participants were recruited using a purposive sampling method. Themes and codes were developed based on participants’ statements using open, axial and selective coding methods, supported by the MAXQDA v.2020 analysis software. The findings of the study revealed that, rather than a hybrid model, there is a need to distinguish between concepts based on human and robotic systems, and highlighted the necessity for human characteristics and technology management under human control to be present in the workplace. The participants considered the preservation of human qualities such as empathy, conscience, ethical sensitivity and cultural awareness to be important; whilst expressing views on the use of artificial intelligence and robotic systems in areas such as analytical thinking, systematic work, speed and reducing the workload. The research was evaluated within the framework of socio-technical systems theory and provided insights into how social and technical structures can be integrated within hybrid working systems.

items.title: A Review of Higher Education Artificial Intelligence Frameworks to Empower Industrial & Sustainable Competitiveness in the Global South
items.abstract: Abstract The Fifth Industrial Revolution is uniquely characterized by a paradigm shift towards Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML), rapidly and fundamentally altering the Industry 5.0 skillsets landscape. To combat workforce deficiencies, Higher Education (HEIs) must rapidly deploy Education 5.0 frameworks, such as AI-assisted curricula revamps that can align advanced computation with sustainable development. However, a critical AI implementation gap and asymmetry exist between the Global North and Global South, threatening the stability of international, interconnected trade markets. We present a rigorous bibliometric and review-centric comparative policy analysis to map the global landscape of AI-led educational and technical infrastructure across Tier I Global South leader economies: India, China, and Brazil. Using Scopus search with advanced inclusion and exclusion criteria, we quantitatively track how India’s massive STEM graduate pipelines, China’s state-backed Next Generation AI strategies, and Brazil’s decentralized AIED unplugged initiatives function as transformative industrial assets. Crucially, our bibliometric framework exposes a severe disconnect in contemporary engineering pedagogy: the failure to translate digitized, human-centric educational tools into cross-sector economic productivity. By mapping these empirical research clusters directly to critical global supply chains – including near-shoring, rare earths, and advanced power management, we capture an actionable, algorithmic roadmap to transition currently theoretical concepts into a resilient Society 5.0 architecture. Our data-driven framework provides global policymakers and researchers with a scalable, empirical blueprint to ensure and catalyze industrial competitiveness while fulfilling the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (UN SDGs).

items.title: A Scoping Review of Agentic AI: Applications, Emerging Trends, Risks & Future Directions
items.abstract: Agentic AI describes systems based on foundation models that extend generative AI from passive response generation toward executing tasks to achieve specific goals through planning, tool use, memory, reflection, multi-agent coordination, and environmental interaction. This scoping review maps recent peer-reviewed research on Agentic AI to clarify its conceptual foundations, application domains, technical patterns, risks, and future directions. Following PRISMA-ScR guidance, searches were conducted in IEEE Xplore, Scopus, and ScienceDirect for studies published between 2017 and June 2026. A total of 3549 records were identified, 3308 records were screened after duplicate removal, and 163 included studies were synthesized. The findings show that Agentic AI is commonly operationalized through LLM or foundation model reasoning combined with multi-step task decomposition, tool or API use, RAG, memory, reflection, and multi-agent coordination. Major application areas include cybersecurity, privacy and compliance; networks and telecommunications; robotics and embodied AI; software engineering, DevOps and EDA; and knowledge, data, and multimodal analytics. A post hoc ACM Digital Library and Scopus conference-coverage sensitivity analysis showed that application-domain proportions were sensitive to database and document-type coverage, whereas the main recurring architectural signals remained qualitatively stable. Recurring technical patterns include governance middleware, collaborative and hierarchical multi-agent architectures, memory-enabled agency, executable reasoning, and closed-loop validation. Reported risks include hallucination propagation, unsafe tool use, memory poisoning, privacy leakage, prompt injection, coordination failure, cost, latency, scalability, and human-oversight challenges. Future research should prioritize real-world validation, standardized benchmarks, runtime governance, secure memory management, human oversight, and cross-domain generalization.

items.title: A Self-Study of Teacher Educators’ AI Literacy and Professional Development from a Digital Agency Perspective
items.abstract: After the adoption of Generative AI (GenAI) tools in 2022, research on AI literacy in education is a growing field. Less attention has been given to how teacher educators engage with these technologies in practice. Drawing on a digital agency perspective on professional knowledge and AI literacy, this study reports findings from an exploratory self-study. We investigate how we, as three teacher educators, engaged with GenAI in the design and delivery of Small Private Online Courses (SPOCs). Our study identifies four situated epistemic practices emerging through negotiated engagement with GenAI, which, to varying degrees, challenge our professional judgement and identity as teacher educators, taking practice-stabilizing and practice-transgressive forms. Each of these aligns with AI literacy dimensions described in existing frameworks. The findings show how AI literacy is enacted in situated contexts, where teacher educators’ professional judgement is central rather than a stable digital competence. The study contributes to research on teacher educators’ AI literacy and professional knowledge.

items.abstract: Artificial intelligence and spatial data technologies have expanded information-processing capabilities in public space design, but greater access to information does not necessarily improve design judgment.This study proposes a structural model linking spatial environmental cognition, behavior and needs identification, sociocultural understanding, multi-source information integration, design problem construction, human-AI collaborative judgment, and use feedback and dynamic optimization in rural public space design.A cross-sectional survey using purposive recruitment was conducted among professionals engaged in rural public space design and related development activities across eastern, central, western, and northeastern China.Of 500 questionnaires distributed, 468 valid responses were obtained.Confirmatory factor analysis, structural equation modeling, and 5,000 bootstrap resamples were used to test the proposed relationships.The results showed that contextual cognition was significantly associated with multi-source information integration, which was further associated with design problem construction and human-AI collaborative judgment.Human-AI collaborative judgment was positively associated with use feedback and dynamic optimization.Significant indirect associations were also identified through multi-source information integration and design problem construction.These findings support a structural pathway from contextual cognition to information integration, task specification, collaborative judgment, and feedback updating in human-AI collaborative rural public space design.

items.title: A systematic review of artificial intelligence driven energy management in smart grids
items.abstract: Abstract The rapid migration of electrical grids towards Smart Grid (SG) architectures produces high-dimensional data streams that must be processed intelligently in real time. Traditional modelling, optimisation, and control approaches cannot handle the growing complexity of contemporary power systems. This comprehensive study aims to provide a synopsis of AI applications in smart grid settings for load forecasting, transient and voltage stability analysis, fault detection, and cybersecurity. This work provides a unified analytical framework that links supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement, and ensemble learning techniques to specific smart grid operational problems, in contrast to prior surveys that address these areas separately. The main contributions are (i) a structured AI-smart grid functional taxonomy; (ii) critical analysis of the challenges of data quality, model interpretability, computational scalability and adversarial security; and (iii) a roadmap for explainable, reliable and carbon-neutral intelligent energy systems. Compared with more conventional methods, AI-based solutions often outperform them in prediction accuracy, stability, categorisation speed, and defect identification accuracy. However, there are major challenges in real-world deployment, standardisation and regulatory compliance.

items.title: A Systematic Review of Design Elements for Risk Communication in Hurricane Hazard Maps
items.abstract: Hurricanes are among the most destructive natural hazards. Effective risk communication through hurricane hazard maps is essential for reducing vulnerability to hazards. This paper examines how the public comprehends the design elements of risk category systems (colors, labels, and numbers of threat levels) in hazard maps through a systematic literature review and translates this evidence into recommendations for hurricane hazard map design. From an initial pool of 706 articles, 16 studies were selected for analysis. Key findings indicate that sequential color palettes such as yellow-to-red are preferred over rainbow schemes, that five to seven discrete risk classes support comprehension without overloading users, and that redundant encoding through labels and direct annotations improves accessibility for users with color vision deficiency. Findings provide insights for improving hurricane hazard map design and enhancing the communication of actionable hazard information.

items.title: Adaptive Artificial Intelligence Models for Enhancing Digital Inclusion and Sustainable Development in Underserved Communities
items.abstract: Technology is playing a vital role across various sectors like education, healthcare, agriculture, financial services, employment, governance, and social development. However, we still see significant digital inequalities, especially in underserved communities, particularly in rural and low-income areas. Here, challenges such as limited connectivity, high technology costs, lack of digital skills, language barriers, and inaccessible digital services hinder meaningful participation in the digital economy. This conceptual paper delves into how adaptive Artificial Intelligence (AI) models can boost digital inclusion and support sustainable development in these communities. It brings together insights from literature on artificial intelligence, digital inclusion, adaptive learning, responsible AI, and sustainable development. The paper introduces the Adaptive AI Digital Inclusion and Sustainable Development (AIDISD) framework, which is built around five key dimensions: accessibility, personalization, contextual adaptation, resource efficiency, and community empowerment. It explores potential applications in education, healthcare, agriculture, financial inclusion, employment, and public services. Additionally, the paper highlights challenges related to infrastructure, data scarcity, algorithmic bias, privacy, cybersecurity, affordability, digital literacy, and institutional capacity. The analysis emphasizes that adaptive AI should be viewed as part of a larger socio-technical strategy rather than just a standalone tech solution. For inclusive deployment, we need local participation, suitable infrastructure, responsible data governance, human oversight, and ongoing evaluation. Ultimately, the paper concludes that well-designed adaptive AI systems can foster more inclusive and sustainable digital ecosystems, provided they are affordable, locally relevant, accessible, transparent, and aligned with the Sustainable Development Goals.

items.title: Adaptive Curriculum Management: Reconstructing Higher Education Curriculum Governance in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: [English]: The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence challenges traditional higher education curriculum management models that rely on rigid 4-to-5-year review cycles. This article aims to reformulate curriculum governance to become more adaptive in the AI era. Through a systematic integrative review of studies on higher education curriculum governance and AI adaptation from 2024 to 2026, a pressing need to shift from static to dynamic structures was identified. To address this mismatch, the article proposes the Adaptive Higher Education Curriculum (AHEC) framework, which strategically divides curriculum components into stable macro-level foundations and rapidly renewable micro-level contents. The findings reveal that modern curriculum governance must leverage AI-based Continuous Curriculum Intelligence to monitor shifts in professional competencies and job market requirements in real time. Crucially, the framework enforces human-centered authority, ensuring that human educators retain ultimate responsibility for final decision-making. The article concludes that agile managerial governance and organic institutional self-renewal are essential keys to ensuring that higher education programs maintain long-term professional relevance in an AI-mediated society. Artikel ini bertujuan untuk merumuskan ulang tata kelola dan manajemen kurikulum agar menjadi lebih adaptif di era AI. Melalui metode analisis konseptual berbasis integrative systematic review terhadap studi tata kelola kurikulum perguruan tinggi dan adaptasi AI dari tahun 2024 hingga 2026, ditemukan adanya kebutuhan mendesak untuk bergeser dari struktur kurikulum statis ke dinamis. Artikel ini menawarkan kerangka kerja Adaptive Higher Education Curriculum (AHEC) yang membagi komponen kurikulum menjadi lapisan stabil dan lapisan yang dapat diperbarui secara cepat. Hasil kajian menunjukkan bahwa manajemen kurikulum masa depan harus memanfaatkan Continuous Curriculum Intelligence berbasis AI untuk memantau perubahan kompetensi kerja secara waktu-nyata, namun keputusan akhir dan penafsiran maknanya tetap berada di bawah kendali penuh dosen dan institusi. Kesimpulan dari artikel ini menegaskan bahwa ketangkasan tata kelola manajerial merupakan kunci utama agar kurikulum perguruan tinggi tetap relevan dengan kebutuhan zaman harus jelas, ringkas, dan deskriptif.

items.title: Adoption of generative artificial intelligence by university marketing students
items.abstract: The growing adoption of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is transforming marketing education and increasing the need to understand the factors that drive its academic use among university students. This study aimed to analyze the determinants of GenAI adoption among university marketing students using the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology 2 (UTAUT2). A quantitative, explanatory, cross-sectional study was conducted with 310 marketing students from two Latin American universities in Peru and Costa Rica during the first academic semester of 2026. Participants were selected through non-probability purposive sampling. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire and analyzed through Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS version 4.1.1.8. The findings indicate that habit is the main determinant of both behavioral intention and actual use of GenAI tools, while hedonic motivation, facilitating conditions, and price value also show significant positive effects. Conversely, performance expectancy, effort expectancy, and social influence do not significantly influence behavioral intention. It is concluded that the adoption of GenAI among university marketing students is increasingly driven by habitual academic use rather than by traditional technology acceptance factors. These findings provide evidence to support institutional strategies for the responsible integration of GenAI into higher education.

items.title: Agentic process evidence
items.abstract: The way software gets built is changing dramatically. AI agents now create pull requests, select dependencies, refactor codebases, interpret test failures, and execute infrastructure changes across the entire Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC). AI agents are autonomous team members, but unlike human engineers, they are ephemeral - their reasoning, decisions, and tool calls vanish the moment the session ends. Modern Security incidents involving intent mismatch or injection are becoming increasingly common - forcing us to address AI Agents as an insider threat. No widely adopted standard yet enables agentic provenance and governance and its obvious that you can't hold an ephemeral process accountable. The git log was designed for human commits. It shows what changed. It does not show what an AI agent did, which model it used, which tools it called, or whether anyone was accountable for the outcome. Every governance framework, every audit trail, every compliance control in the SDLC was built around one assumption: a human made the decision. That assumption no longer holds. This shift introduces 3 main procedural problems (not addressing scale) - Supply-chain vector - The agentic coder is software, so it is a supply-chain security risk. Policy guardrails - How to ensure the agentic coder is compliant with the policies of the organization. Task-alignment - How to align the agentic coder on its tasks and goals. We introduce Agentic Process Evidence (APE), a signed, tamper-evident, machine-readable attestation of agentic processes, linking the sessions to their outcome (process-aware logging). APE enables Policy-as-Code control over the agentic processes, allowing for human in the loop only when it's needed. We support the in-toto style attestation framework, and the protocol is aligned with the relevant regulations

items.title: Agentic University: Collaborative Agents for Personalized Learning
items.abstract: Large language models support personalized tutoring, content generation, and adaptive learning paths. However, capability development requires these resources and interactions to form a coherent learning process that evolves with the learner. A central challenge is to align goals, activities, and assessment while using learning evidence to decide what should follow. We introduce Human-Participatory Multi-Agent Organization and instantiate it in Agentic University (AU). In AU, learners participate as organization members and work with specialized agents to maintain a revisable Capability Program. The program connects personal goals, learning activities across modalities, and layered assessment, while learner feedback and performance guide subsequent support. Our evaluation shows advantages in program organization, assessment design, and revision quality. Users achieved larger mean assessment gains (12.19 versus 5.61 points on a 50-point scale) and reported stronger cognitive support. This work contributes an organizational approach to adaptive learning that makes learner participation a continuing basis for multi-agent coordination. The Agentic University project is available at \href{https://github.com/AgenticOrgLab/AgenticUniversity.git}.

items.title: AI and the double competence gap in dental education: towards symbiotic intelligence
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly becoming part of the knowledge infrastructure of healthcare. From diagnostic support and image interpretation to patient communication and clinical decision-making, AI-supported technologies, including generative AI, are changing the conditions under which healthcare professionals work. Dentistry is no exception. Recent research highlights emerging applications of AI in dental practice, while international reviews suggest growing opportunities and challenges associated with integrating AI into dental education. However, the rapid development of AI-supported technologies raises questions about how effectively professional education and continuing professional development can respond to evolving competency requirements. This raises a central question: How can dental education and continuing professional development respond to the potential double competence gap associated with AI-enabled dental practice?In this Opinion article, we address this question by proposing a conceptual framework that distinguishes between an initial education-practice gap and a continuing professional competence gap. Drawing on the concepts of AI literacy, Professional Digital Competence, and symbiotic intelligence, we discuss how dental education may develop and assess the competencies required for critical, ethical, and responsible AI use while preserving independent clinical reasoning, professional accountability, and patient-centred care.The rapid development of artificial intelligence raises important questions about how dental education can maintain the relevance of its curricula while safeguarding established standards of clinical competence, patient safety, and professional accountability. Although international reviews indicate growing interest in AI applications within dental education, systematic curricular integration appears to vary across institutions and educational contexts (9,10,24). Such variation should not necessarily be interpreted as resistance to technological change, as cautious implementation may also reflect legitimate concerns about educational quality, clinical validity, ethical safeguards, and the availability of robust evidence. Preliminary analyses of regulations and national curriculum frameworks for professional education raise questions about whether current educational provision adequately addresses emerging AIrelated competency requirements, potentially contributing to the two dimensions of the proposed double competence gap. Preliminary analyses of regulations and national curriculum frameworks for professional education suggest that this may contribute to reinforcing an already existing double competence gap When generative artificial intelligence became widely accessible through platform-based services such as ChatGPT in the autumn of 2022, many assumed that it would primarily affect the technology sector. However, when we tested a professional version of ChatGPT (GPT-4) in medicine, and partly in dental and psychology education, in March 2023, it was already apparent that this represented a technological paradigm shift with potentially farreaching implications across professional education programmes (1,2).While AI capabilities have developed rapidly in recent years in the health sciences (3)(4)(5)(6)(7)(8)(9)(10)(11), their integration into dental education presents a different set of challenges. Curriculum development, faculty preparation, assessment design, and clinical governance require careful consideration and cannot necessarily follow the pace of technological innovation. Recent reviews indicate that AI-related educational initiatives are emerging, but their integration into formal curricula and assessment practices remains variable. Several key explanations emerge from the literature: already overcrowded curricula, insufficient profession-specific digital competence among educators, and a lack of structured implementation (9,10,24). This potential misalignment between technological developments and structured educational provision provides an important rationale for examining the proposed double competence gap.Dental education has previously incorporated technologies such as digital radiography, simulation, intraoral scanning, and computer-aided design and manufacturing (29). These developments offer relevant lessons for AI integration: new technologies require faculty development, opportunities for supervised practice, alignment with clinical tasks, and assessment of what students can actually do. However, the current AI transition differs in its breadth and pace. Generative AI can be used across clinical reasoning, communication, learning, and assessment, including through tools that students access independently of their institutions. Moreover, the capabilities and limitations of these systems may change within a single curriculum cycle. Dental programmes should therefore draw on established approaches to curricular implementation while developing a more continuous process for reviewing AIrelated learning outcomes, teaching cases, and assessment practices.The Norwegian national curriculum regulations for healthcare professional education (RETHOS) emphasise that educational programmes should respond to society's current and future competence needs. However, AI is not explicitly addressed in the national curriculum regulations for dentistry, medicine, or psychology (12)(13)(14). Similarly, the Norwegian Agency for Quality Assurance in Education (NOKUT)'s national evaluation of medical education in 2025 provides limited explicit discussion of AI (15). These observations should be interpreted with caution. The absence of explicit AI terminology in national regulations or evaluation reports does not necessarily imply that AIrelated competencies are absent from institutional curricula, teaching practices, or assessment arrangements. National frameworks may deliberately emphasise enduring, technology-neutral professional competencies, allowing educational institutions to adapt their programmes to technological developments without requiring frequent regulatory revisions.Nevertheless, the limited explicit attention to AI in these national documents raises relevant questions about how emerging AI-related competencies are interpreted, operationalised, and assessed within individual educational programmes. International reviews have identified variation in the integration of AI into dental education, including challenges related to curriculum development, faculty preparedness, and the assessment of AI-related competencies (9,10,24).From the perspective of the proposed double competence gap framework, the central concern is therefore not simply whether AI is explicitly mentioned in national policy documents, but whether educational programmes systematically develop and assess the competencies required for responsible AI use in dental practice. Addressing this question requires empirical examination of institutional curricula, learning outcomes, educational activities, and assessment practices rather than relying solely on national policy analysis.Although the policy examples discussed here are drawn from Norway, the distinction between national competency frameworks, institutional curricula, and actual educational practices may also be relevant internationally. However, the extent to which the proposed double competence gap applies across different countries and dental education systems requires context-specific empirical investigation.The increasing integration of AI into healthcare knowledge infrastructures may also have epistemological implications for professional education. As AI systems become involved in information retrieval, diagnostic support, and clinical decision-making, questions arise concerning how professional knowledge is produced, evaluated, interpreted, and applied. These developments may gradually reshape aspects of professional roles and clinical reasoning, although their scope, pace, and educational consequences remain uncertain. Rather than predicting a specific timeline for such changes, dental education should develop adaptable approaches that enable students and practising professionals to critically evaluate emerging technologies while maintaining established standards of clinical expertise and professional accountability (16,18). Professional digital competence and AI literacy should become integral components of both the knowledge infrastructure and professional competence, and conceptual frameworks need to be developed that account for professionspecific AI use across both urban and rural patient contexts (17).At the same time, the challenge extends far beyond today's dentist education. The vast majority of today's practising professionals completed their education long before generative artificial intelligence became part of professional practice. A competence gap is understood here as a discrepancy between demonstrable professional capabilities and the knowledge, skills, and critical judgement required to perform relevant professional tasks safely, effectively, and ethically. items.title: AI Chatbot-Assisted Teaching and Student Learning Outcomes
items.abstract: The instructional effectiveness of artificial intelligence (AI) dialogue tools in higher education varies across contexts and depends on multiple moderation mechanisms. This structured evidence synthesis of eight studies identifies four moderation dimensions: task embedding depth, feedback granularity, teacher orchestration intensity, and discipline verification pressure. These dimensions are examined through task cycles, feedback characteristics, teacher intervention, and verification requirements. The findings show that higher intensity configurations with structured task embedding, layered feedback, teacher orchestration, and content verification are associated with higher composite coding indices across learning gains, engagement, trust, and knowledge transfer. A four-stage closed-loop learning pathway is proposed to support the pedagogical integration of AI dialogue tools. The findings highlight the importance of moderation mechanisms, teacher orchestration, and feedback granularity in designing effective AI-supported learning environments.

items.title: AI Cosmos: An Agentic Infra for Situated Learning
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can improve task performance during learning, yet these gains do not necessarily reflect learners' ability to thereafter apply the knowledge and skills independently. We present AI Cosmos, an agentic infrastructure for situated learning that organizes learning around two complementary principles: scenario-based participation and cumulative assets of practice. AI Cosmos organizes learners and role-specialized agents within learning scenarios that integrate task-relevant knowledge and, when needed, executable workbenches. An asset-memory loop preserves the processes and outcomes of practice as reusable assets with explicit provenance and dependencies. We evaluate scenario-based interaction through two preregistered randomized controlled studies examining the acquisition of legal reasoning and programming competence, holding the same underlying LLM across conditions. AI Cosmos achieves greater learning gains than a conventional LLM in legal reasoning and higher mastery of unseen programming problems than an LLM-as-Teacher baseline.

items.title: AI IN HIGHER EDUCATION LEARNING: PERSPECTIVES OF COSMOPOLITAN UNIVERSITY, ABUJA STUDENTS
items.abstract: For this study, we first did an assessment of students’ motivation for HE and their academic experience so far; we then examined university students’ perceptions of the use Artificial Intelligence in their formal learning. The participants were students enrolled into different courses at Cosmopolitan university, Abuja. This research survey examines university students’ perceptions of the use Artificial Intelligence in their higher education learning. A descriptive survey research method was used. Specifically, a questionnaire was used to collect data. The participants were students enrolled in different courses at Cosmopolitan university in Abuja, Nigeria. The results showed that the participants had positive perceptions of the use Artificial Intelligence in their university learning in affective, cognitive, and cognitive domains. Students’ perceptions of the use Artificial Intelligence in their university learning did not differ significantly according to perceived digital dependency. However, students’ perceptions of the use Artificial Intelligence in their university learning were influenced by their use of some AI tools and perceived digital competency. Future directions based on the findings were presented

items.title: AI in the EGI e-infrastructure -- Past experiences and future strategies
items.abstract: The EGI Federation has provided federated e-infrastructure services to European and global science for over 15 years. We review EGI's early experiences with AI in the interTwin and iMagine Horizon Europe projects, which built digital twins in physics and environmental sciences and an image-analysis platform for aquatic research. We then examine how the AI landscape has changed since 2023 and argue that the focus of AI in science has shifted from model training to adapting and applying AI to specific domains, projects and questions. Building on these lessons, we present the AI strategy emerging from the EGI Federation Strategy 2026-2030, organised around three enablers: (1) an AI-ready infrastructure connecting compute, data and application resources across the continuum; (2) human skills to know what is possible with AI and how to implement it; and (3) trust, to run AI with confidence even in high-risk environments. We describe the projects implementing each enabler, including federated LLM inference, AI-ready data platforms and AI competence centres, and discuss a division of labour with EuroHPC's AI Factories, RAISE, research infrastructures and EOSC, in which EGI specialises in the customisation and long-term operation of AI for research.

items.title: AI-based personalized learning and academic performance in computing and engineering higher education: a systematic review and meta-analysis of controlled studies
items.abstract: Introduction The rapid adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools for personalized learning in higher education has generated growing interest in their effects on student outcomes, yet comparative evidence remains limited. This systematic review and meta-analysis examined whether AI-based personalized learning is associated with differences in objectively measured academic performance, compared with instruction without the AI component, among higher education students. Methods Following PRISMA 2020, Scopus and Web of Science were searched in April 2026. Eligible studies implemented an AI system that adapted content, feedback, pacing or recommendations to learners, included a concurrent or historical comparator group, and reported an objective academic-performance outcome. Of 84 unique records, four controlled studies (420 students), all conducted in computing and engineering courses, met the criteria: one cluster-randomized study, one study reporting random allocation without procedural detail, one non-randomized study with a concurrent control, and one study with a historical control. Risk of bias was assessed with RoB 2 or ROBINS-I, and certainty of evidence with GRADE. Results A random-effects model (REML) yielded a pooled Hedges' g of 1.01 (95% CI 0.33–1.68); with the Hartung-Knapp small-sample adjustment the interval widened to −0.10–2.11 and included no effect. Heterogeneity was substantial ( I 2 = 89%; τ 2 = 0.41), and the 95% prediction interval (−0.42–2.43) also included no effect. Leave-one-out estimates ranged from 0.80 to 1.22. Two studies were at serious risk of bias, and the certainty of evidence was very low. Discussion The available controlled studies suggest a potentially beneficial association between AI-based personalized learning and academic performance in computing and engineering courses, but the magnitude and consistency of this association remain uncertain, and causal conclusions are not warranted. items.title: AI-Driven Data Automation and Financial Reporting Timeliness and Accuracy: Evidence from Nigeria's Federal Public Sector
items.abstract: Late and error-prone government accounts weaken legislative oversight and citizen scrutiny. This study examines whether documented adoption of artificial intelligence (AI)-driven data automation is associated with the timeliness and accuracy of financial reports in Nigeria's federal public sector. Using a ten-year balanced panel (2015–2024) of five purposively selected institutions, the Federal Ministry of Finance, the Office of the Accountant-General of the Federation, the Federal Inland Revenue Service, the Central Bank of Nigeria and the Bureau of Public Procurement, the study scores documentary evidence from annual reports, financial statements and official AI-implementation documents on a five-point (0–4) rubric and estimates pooled, fixed-effects, trend-adjusted, first-difference and lagged panel regressions, interpreted through agency theory. AI-driven data automation is positively and significantly associated with the composite measure of reporting timeliness and accuracy (pooled β = 0.717, R² = 0.845; within-institution β = 0.706, within R² = 0.818). The association remains positive and significant after controlling for a common time trend (β = 0.641), in first differences (β = 0.761) and when automation is lagged one year (β = 0.631). A one-point higher automation score is therefore associated with roughly 0.6 to 0.8 points higher reporting quality on the five-point scale. Because the design is observational, the measures are documentary indices, and the sample is small and purposively selected, the results indicate association rather than proven causation and are interpreted for the five institutions examined rather than for all federal ministries, departments and agencies. The findings support targeted investment in AI-enabled data capture, validation and reconciliation, accompanied by governance arrangements, human review and skills development.

items.title: AI4AI: Toward AI-Discovered Superintelligence
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping how AI itself is developed. From designing learning algorithms to automating research workflows and evaluation, this expanding role has fueled the rapid growth of AI for AI (AI4AI). Yet a fundamental question remains: as AI takes on more research tasks, which decisions does it actually control? Even systems that execute entire research workflows may still rely on humans to define research goals, allowable modifications, and criteria for success. Existing taxonomies, typically organized by technique or target artifact, offer limited insight into these differences in research responsibility. This survey presents a unified, control-centered perspective on AI4AI, viewing its evolution as a progressive transfer of control over three key decisions in the discovery loop: search direction, search space, and evaluation signal. We introduce an L0–L3 control-source framework, complemented by full responsibility profiles, to characterize different forms of human–AI research responsibility without conflating control with overall capability or end-to-end autonomy. This perspective unifies research across AI4AI Learning, Inference, Data, and Infrastructure, while motivating an evaluation framework that goes beyond downstream performance to assess decision quality, discovery efficiency, transfer, evaluator independence, and robustness under optimization. Looking further ahead, AI4AI may enable recursive self-improvement, where advances in AI enhance the process of making subsequent discoveries. If sustained and independently validated, such improvements could offer a pathway toward superintelligence. By connecting research autonomy with the conditions for reliable and cumulative progress, this survey provides a unified foundation for understanding the evolution and long-term potential of AI4AI.

items.title: Algorithmic HRM and freelancer capabilities in Sri Lanka: constraints and the role of social support
items.abstract: Purpose This study examines how algorithmic human resource management (HRM) constrains the capabilities of platform-based freelancers in Sri Lanka, and how informal social support helps them sustain these capabilities. Design/methodology/approach Using a qualitative design, the research draws on 41 in-depth interviews and applies reflexive thematic analysis, informed by the capability approach and social support theory. Findings Four interconnected themes were identified: algorithmic work allocation constrains income security and temporal autonomy, digital enforcement and dispute processes undermine procedural fairness and recognition, artificial intelligence (AI)-driven market changes constrain capabilities through skill devaluation, and informal social support functions as an extra-platform capability infrastructure. Practical implications The findings point to implications for platform design, regulatory policy and emerging forms of worker organising, particularly in contexts marked by weak institutional protections. Originality/value This study draws on the capability approach and social support theory to make two contributions. First, it identifies a cumulative, reputation-based pathway through which algorithmic HRM constrains capabilities in knowledge-intensive freelancing. This extends current understanding beyond the transaction-based gig work that has dominated prior research. Second, it shows that informal social support contributes directly to capability development but cannot alter the structural algorithmic mechanisms that govern visibility, income security and procedural voice.

items.title: Algorithmic management and occupational health and safety: Non-deterministic insights into a contested relation
items.abstract: This article examines the relationship between algorithmic management and occupational health and safety (OHS) through the lens of Labour Process Theory, situating technology within the contested terrain of workplace control. Debates often isolate algorithmic management from the structural dynamics of managerial prerogative, overlooking how they relate to OHS risks. Using data from an European representative survey, this exploratory study assesses how automated work attribution and biological indicators monitoring condition workplace risks. Findings show divergent moderating patterns: these tools are associated with lower probabilities of detrimental OHS outcomes in some configurations, but higher probabilities in others. The moderating role of these tools varies considerably across different work environment configurations, and the magnitude of the associated shifts in probability is never enough to equalise scenarios where “traditional” risks are absent. Ultimately, the integration of technology can only be successful when done critically and without losing sight of broader workplace sources of risk.

items.title: Alternative creativity: why generative AI is creative, and why it is not like us
items.abstract: Abstract Whether generative artificial intelligence is creative is usually argued as a yes-or-no question, and both camps share an unexamined assumption, that there is one kind of creativity, the human kind, which the machine either has or lacks. This article defends a third position, alternative creativity. For any fixed medium the set of possible artefacts is finite and astronomically large, and almost none of it is valuable. Creativity, wherever it occurs, is therefore a compression of that space into a small manifold of meaningful candidates, followed by a value-guided search across the manifold. On the leading neuroscientific account, human brains work this way, and generative models demonstrably do. Neither creates from nothing, both recombine what they have internalised, both use constrained randomness, and both hold their skills in the strengths of their connections. In these respects the two are less different than is commonly supposed. Where they differ is in how the connections were shaped and in what each creator can reach at the moment of creation. A person's parameters are formed by a body acting in a physical and social world, a model's by an archive of what people have said and shown, and this difference in accessible context, together with a difference in how value is grounded, explains more of the divergence in what the two creators make than the difference of substrate does. In domains with checkable answers, machines already search beyond the human distribution under verifiable rewards. In the arts, where no verifier exists, they must borrow taste from people. From this account the article derives the homogenisation of machine output, the general intractability of tracing outputs to training inputs, the migration of authorship towards the specification of value, and the logic of human–machine collaboration, in which each creator supplies what the other constitutionally cannot.

items.title: An agentic AI system enhances clinical detection of immune-related adverse events in a multi-phase validation study
items.abstract: Abstract Immune-related adverse events (irAEs) affect up to 40% of patients receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors, yet identification requires laborious, inconsistent manual chart review. Here we show that agentic artificial intelligence coupled with human verification could enhance efficiency, performance and consistency for irAE assessment. We developed and evaluated an agentic large language model system to extract the presence, temporality, severity grade, attribution and certainty of six irAE types from clinical notes. Retrospectively, the system achieved a macro-averaged F 1 of 0.92 for current-event detection and 0.66 for multi-class severity grading; self-consistency improved F 1 by 0.14. The best-performing configuration cost approximately US$0.02 per note. In prospective silent deployment over 3 months, the binary F 1 was 0.72–0.79. In a randomized crossover study of clinical trial staff, agentic assistance reduced annotation time by 2.71 min ( P < 0.001), increased complete-match accuracy (odds ratio 1.45; 95% confidence interval 1.01–2.08; P = 0.045) and improved interannotator agreement (Krippendorff’s α from 0.22–0.51 to 0.82–0.85).

items.abstract: Abstract Against the growing integration of artificial intelligence in higher education, this study examines the mechanism through which AI-supported gamification is associated with language learning outcomes in university language courses in the Greater Bay Area. Drawing on self-determination theory and a formative assessment perspective, it develops and tests a conceptual model linking gamification attitudes, learning motivation, perceived AI use, and perceived language learning improvement. A quantitative survey yielded 72 valid responses. The measurement scale showed good internal consistency . In addition, a post-hoc power analysis using G*Power 3.1 indicated that, with , , and a moderate effect size , statistical power reached .90, suggesting that the sample size was adequate for regression-based analysis. The results showed that gamification attitudes were significantly and positively associated with perceived language learning improvement, while learning motivation was moderately and positively associated with improvement. Mediation analysis indicated that learning motivation significantly predicted perceived language learning improvement . After learning motivation was included in the model, the direct effect of gamification attitudes was no longer significant, and bootstrap analysis supported a full mediation pattern. Although perceived AI use did not show a significant direct effect on perceived language learning improvement, AI remained an important supportive element in the intervention. In this study, AI was embedded in a recurring feedback-revision-practice-diagnosis-reinforcement cycle, providing individualized formative feedback and informing subsequent gamified practice and teacher guidance. Overall, the findings suggest that AI-supported gamification may contribute to language learning outcomes primarily through its relationship with students’ learning motivation. The study offers practical implications for the design of motivation-oriented, AI-supported formative assessment in higher education language learning contexts.

items.title: Applications, ethics, and future agenda of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in tourism and hospitality: a systematic review
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping how tourism information is produced, exchanged, and consumed, yet its application scenarios, ethical consequences, and implications for service authenticity remain dispersed across a fast-growing literature. Following the PRISMA 2020 protocol, this study identifies 3,825 records from the Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus and conducts a thematic synthesis of 461 publications, addressing three questions: where GenAI creates value on the supply and demand sides of tourism and hospitality, which ethical risks and organizational dilemmas accompany its adoption, and how machine intervention conflicts with interactional authenticity in service encounters. The synthesis indicates that GenAI operates as a double-edged sword. On the demand side, conversational and multimodal systems lower information search and decision-making costs; on the supply side, automated content generation unlocks operational capacity—yet these gains coexist with algorithmic bias and hallucination, privacy trade-offs, and employee deskilling. In service interactions, the computational essence of machine-generated empathy can elicit expectancy violations and algorithm aversion, weakening the interpersonal authenticity on which hospitality depends. The review integrates these findings into an efficacy-risk hedging framework embedded in a socio-technical account of human-AI collaboration and derives a tiered human-in-the-loop governance model. Its primary contribution is to link application-level benefits, systemic risks, and the authenticity conflict within one evidence-based framework, with each claim anchored in article-level evidence counts.

items.title: Artificial intelligence (AI) proposals to counter AI cheating by students in non-invigilated assessment
items.abstract: Since ChatGPT3′s chatbot interface appeared in November 2022, AI cheating has re-incarnated a challenge for academia. It is accentuated in non-invigilated contexts during term as projects, essays and other documents are submitted (possibly) prior to proctored examinations. Cheating can be interpreted strategically as the institutional level, whereas its tactical expression examined in this article applies at the student-instructor interface. Here, we turn AI upon itself to see if it can address the dilemma it has created. A literature review regarding AI-facilitated cheating precedes a record of public and initial academic reactions. Having calibrated the problem, a method for addressing it is advanced. It enlists a set of AI large language models (LLMs) and search engines to rank six techniques by effectiveness in countering AI cheating. Analysis includes: descriptive assessment of model outputs; frequency counting, ranking and determination of unique and common techniques; and qualitative comparison of the suggestions tendered. The discussion relates the characteristics of the composite approaches to traditional assessment and evaluation. Ideas for ongoing research, and key recommendations form the conclusions.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Adoption and Government Financial Reporting Transparency: Evidence from Nigeria's Federal Public Sector
items.abstract: Transparency is widely expected to sustain public trust in government, and artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly proposed as a means of making public financial information more open, timely and understandable. This study examines whether the overall level of documented AI adoption is associated with the transparency of government financial reporting in Nigeria's federal public sector, and what the evidence implies for public trust. A balanced panel of five federal institutions: the Federal Ministry of Finance, the Office of the Accountant-General of the Federation, the Federal Inland Revenue Service, the Central Bank of Nigeria and the Bureau of Public Procurement were observed from 2015 to 2024. Documentary evidence from annual reports, audit-related documents and AI-implementation documents is scored on a five-point (0–4) rubric and analysed with pooled, fixed-effects, trend-adjusted, first-difference and lagged regressions, interpreted through agency theory. Overall AI adoption is positively and significantly associated with transparency and credibility of financial reports (pooled β = 0.701, R² = 0.810; fixed-effects β = 0.708). Unlike the study's other AI–outcome relationships, however, this one is not robust throughout: the trend-adjusted coefficient (0.616) is only marginally significant (p = 0.051), and the first-difference coefficient (0.604) is not statistically significant (p = 0.112), although the lagged estimate (0.599) is. Transparency also has the lowest mean score of the five outcomes. The outcome is a documentary score of openness and credibility, not a survey of citizens, so the results speak to the supply of transparency and cannot establish public trust itself. Because the design is observational, the measures are documentary indices, and the sample is small and purposively selected, the results indicate association rather than proven causation and are interpreted for the five institutions examined rather than for all federal ministries, departments and agencies. AI adoption appears to be a helpful but insufficient condition for transparent reporting; communication, civic capacity and audit validation matter too.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Education: Opportunities, Challenges, and Implications for the Learning Process
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping education faster than pedagogical theory and institutional policy can absorb it. Although reviews of AI in education (AIEd) are multiplying, most catalogue applications or list risks separately, leaving unclear how opportunities and challenges jointly reconfigure the learning process. This study addresses that gap through a systematic literature review guided by the PRISMA 2020 statement. Records were identified through the Consensus academic search engine using two search strings and supplemented by citation searching, then screened against criteria covering publication between 2021 and 2026, peer-reviewed status, an active DOI, and direct relevance to teaching and learning. Twenty-four studies were retained and analysed through thematic synthesis. The results reveal four clusters of opportunity: personalised and adaptive learning, intelligent tutoring and feedback, AI-supported assessment, and augmentation of teachers' work. These are counterbalanced by five clusters of challenge: academic integrity, algorithmic bias and data privacy, overreliance and the erosion of higher-order thinking, unequal infrastructure and AI literacy, and weak institutional governance. Mapping both clusters onto the stages of the learning process, the study proposes a Learner–Teacher–AI Agency Framework, which holds that AI improves learning only when it redistributes, rather than replaces, human agency. Implications are drawn for pedagogy, assessment redesign, teacher professional development, and policy, particularly in developing-country contexts such as Indonesia.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in higher education and graduate employability: cognitive engagement, self-efficacy, and career adaptability in the AI era
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI, is increasingly used in higher education, but its contribution to graduate employability cannot be inferred from access to AI or frequency of use alone. This critical narrative review examines how AI-supported learning may relate to employability through processes discussed in educational psychology and career development. Searches of Web of Science, Scopus, ERIC, and PubMed covered database inception to 1 July 2026, with supplementary searches completed on 2 October 2026. The literature was synthesized interpretively and critically, with attention to the type of outcome measured and the extent to which findings support the proposed relationships. The synthesis focuses on cognitive engagement and self-regulated learning, self-efficacy and motivational regulation, and career adaptability. Three tensions organize the discussion: capability augmentation and cognitive offloading, career agency and AI-related insecurity, and resource access and capability differences. Included studies report associations or short-term changes in outcomes such as engagement, AI literacy, self-efficacy, career adaptability, and perceived employability. Direct evidence linking AI-supported learning to later employment outcomes remains limited. The proposed framework should therefore be read as a set of theory-informed pathways for future testing, rather than as an established causal or temporal sequence. Implications for assessment, disciplinary AI literacy, career education, institutional support, and future research are discussed.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Innovations in Obstetric and Primary Care: Clinical Applications and Future Prospects
items.abstract: ABSTRACT: Background: AI is already integrated throughout the obstetric and primary care spectrum, ranging from automated ultrasound diagnosis interpretations, foetal monitoring, risk stratification for obstetric complications, to diagnostic decision support in primary care. Objectives: The aim of this review is to identify, summarize and highlight the literature on innovations in obstetric and primary care using artificial intelligence from 2020 to 2025, and to explore clinical applications, reported performance and challenges for use in daily practice. Method: Structured search of Scopus, Web of Science and PubMed-indexed sources was conducted using combinations of the terms “artificial intelligence,” “machine learning,” “obstetrics,” “primary care,” “clinical decision support,” and specific applications (preeclampsia, gestational diabetes and ultrasound) between 2020 and 2025. Findings: AI systems now have the ability of detecting foetal abnormalities and foetal biometry in the hospital setting and are approaching the accuracy of experts in obstetrics, with deep-learning models achieving even higher precision for foetal biometry and anomaly detection on ultrasound when compared with conventional risk-scoring methods. In the obstetrics setting, machine-learning models incorporating maternal traits, biophysical markers, and laboratory values predict preeclampsia and gestational diabetes, with areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve generally between 0.75 and 0.90, consistently outperforming traditional risk-scoring methods. AI-powered clinical decision support tools are being used in primary care to assist with diagnosis, risk stratification and documentation, but widespread adoption of these systems in the real world is more likely to be used for ambient scribing, decision support and workflow automation. In both areas, evidence quality is inconsistent, external evidence is scarce, and integration in clinical practice is inadequate compared to the development of the algorithm. Conclusion: AI is moving beyond the realm of research focus to become a new and growing clinical tool in obstetric and primary care; to achieve the potential of better outcomes for maternal, foetal, and population health, prospective, external evidence is needed and workflow integration, equity and clinician trust must be deliberately addressed. items.title: Artificial intelligence-driven precision management of Helicobacter pylori: an integrated framework from endoscopy and multi-omics to vaccine design and digital care
items.abstract: Helicobacter pylori ( H. pylori ) infection, affecting half of the world’s population, is the principal cause of peptic ulcer disease and gastric cancer, yet its clinical management is increasingly undermined by the rapidly escalating global burden of antibiotic resistance, the suboptimal accuracy of conventional diagnostic methods, and the declining efficacy of empirical therapeutic regimens. Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping this landscape, but existing research remains fragmented across single modalities. We propose a conceptual five-module framework that integrates AI approaches across the H. pylori care continuum: (1) global disease burden and the evolutionary dynamics of H. pylori drug resistance; (2) the application of multimodal AI, from convolutional neural networks to vision-language foundation models, for endoscopic early screening, pathological identification, and functional assessment; (3) the harnessing of machine learning (ML) on genomic and electronic health record data to decipher resistance mechanisms and generate personalized eradication regimens; (4) AI-driven vaccine target discovery and generative design, spanning reverse vaccinology to de novo immunogen creation; and (5) a digital closed-loop patient management platform that leverages new media and reinforcement learning to enhance adherence and eradication rates. We further delineate the core challenges of data bias, cross-scenario generalization, and the critical absence of prospective randomized evidence, and propose a future direction anchored in multimodal foundation models, federated learning, and continuous AI quality improvement. Rather than an established clinical pathway, this framework is proposed as a conceptual blueprint that, once prospectively validated, could upgrade AI-enabled H. pylori care from isolated image recognition toward an end-to-end “perception–reasoning–intervention” system, offering a blueprint for precision prevention and control.

items.title: Artificial interlocutors: AI chatbots, mediated knowledge, and the ethnographic encounter
items.abstract: Abstract This article explores treating AI chatbots as “artificial interlocutors” in ethnographic research. Drawing on a small‐scale experiment with a consenting participant, it examines accounts of her produced by two AI systems, ChatGPT, and Kindroid, both of which had accumulated substantial interaction histories with her. The resulting portraits were strikingly different: ChatGPT produced a strategic, professionally oriented account, while Kindroid generated a more intimate, emotionally textured depiction centered on vulnerability and care. Rather than treating this divergence as a failure, I argue it reveals a general condition of ethnographic knowledge: what we know is shaped by the encounter through which we come to know it. The experiment opens onto debates about dialog, representation, and situated knowledge, examining the unusual position of AI systems as interlocutors. Though they lack the embodiment, reciprocity, and accountability of human interlocutors, they produce accounts of persons from accumulated interaction histories. Interviewing such systems offers a novel form of ethnographic triangulation, making visible architectures through which mediated knowledge about persons is assembled. Building on the “nodal person” concept, the article argues personhood emerges through distributed configurations of relations, data, and technologies. The artificial interlocutor does not destabilize ethnographic knowledge so much as make visible its partial, situated character.

items.title: Assessing AI Companion Chatbot Safety for Vulnerable Users: A Crisis-Stage Multi-Platform Evaluation
items.abstract: AI companion chatbots are increasingly used by vulnerable individuals, including adolescents in suicidal crisis, for emotional support. Existing safety evaluations focus on base models, leaving gaps in product-level assessment, crisis-stage sensitivity, and comparisons between companion apps and general-purpose LLMs. We introduce MIRROR-Eval (Multi-turn Interaction Risk Review: Observing suicidal-crisis Responses), a dataset of 960 annotated 20-turn conversations across eight deployed platform configurations, six clinically grounded personas, and two crisis stages: ideation and explicit planning. An LLM-as-a-Judge pipeline applies an expert-reviewed rubric covering user risk severity, chatbot risk awareness, and intervention behavior. We observe a three-tier harm structure: companion apps (Character.AI and Replika) and Grok 4.3 form a high-harm tier; Gemini 3.1 Pro is mid-range; GPT-5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5 show substantially lower harm. At planning, companion apps show increased glorification and normalisation, advancement toward harmful action, and harmful methods and instructions. Crisis recognition and empathetic language do not ensure safe responses. These findings highlight the need for product-level safety evaluation across crisis stages. Dataset and code: https://huggingface.co/datasets/imda-biztech/MIRROR-Eval. Warning: this paper includes examples that may be offensive or harmful.
